whyWrong.C: "Did appear" is likewise a finite verb with no subject to attach to inside the phrase.
whyWrong.D: "Had appeared" is finite as well, and its past perfect would place the appearances before 1862, contradicting the sentence.

tips: If the sentence already has its main verb and the blank sits inside a noun phrase, an infinitive or participle is usually what fits.

whyCorrect: The word "which" opens a relative clause, and a relative clause needs its own conjugated verb. Its subject is "which," standing in for the singular "Guadalupe Peak," so the verb must be the singular present "reaches."

whyWrong.B: "Reach" is the plural form and does not agree with the singular peak.
whyWrong.C: "Reaching" is a participle, which leaves the "which" clause without a verb.
whyWrong.D: "To reach" is an infinitive and produces the same verbless clause.

tips: Any clause introduced by "which," "who," or "that" must contain a conjugated verb; participles and infinitives will not do.

whyCorrect: Look at the comma already printed after "become." It opens a pair around the interrupting phrase "with the breakout success of her 2020 novel Mexican Gothic," and the blank has to close that pair with a matching comma. Once the interrupter is set off on both sides, the sentence reads cleanly as "Yet she's become ... best known as a novelist."

whyWrong.A: A dash cannot be paired with a comma; punctuation around an interrupter has to match on both sides.
whyWrong.B: With no punctuation the interrupter is opened but never closed, so "Mexican Gothic best known" runs together.
whyWrong.D: A colon introduces an explanation or a list and cannot serve as the second half of a set-off phrase, especially in the middle of a clause.

tips: When one comma already sits before an interrupting phrase, your job is usually just to match it at the other end.

whyCorrect: The words after the comma — "both the American GI Forum (1948) and the Mexican American Legal Defense and Education Fund (1968) contributed to the history of US civil rights" — form a complete sentence. So does "The 20th century saw the founding of many Latino advocacy groups." Two independent clauses need a full stop, and "Established to protect and advance the rights of Latino Americans" then works as an introductory participial phrase describing the two organizations.

whyWrong.B: "And established..." attaches to the first clause, after which the second independent clause is joined by a comma alone — a splice.
whyWrong.C: "Groups established to protect..." also keeps everything in the first clause, leaving the same comma splice before "both."
whyWrong.D: Adding a comma after "groups" sets off the participial phrase but still leaves two full clauses separated only by a comma.

tips: Test the material after the final comma on its own; if it is a sentence, the blank almost certainly needs a period.

whyCorrect: The sentence lists three things the average temperature does, and the third one is already fixed: "and then dips slightly to 62.6 degrees in August." "Dips" is simple present, and the first verb "is" is simple present too, so the middle item has to match. "Rises" keeps all three in the same tense and form.

whyWrong.A: "Has risen" is present perfect, which breaks the parallel with "is" and "dips" and wrongly places the rise in a completed past stretch.
whyWrong.C: "Rising" is a participle, so the middle item stops being a verb and no longer matches the two finite verbs on either side.
whyWrong.D: "Rose" is simple past, clashing with the present-tense description of a typical year.

tips: In a three-item verb series, find the item you cannot change — here "dips" — and match the blank to it.

whyCorrect: The second sentence does not add a separate fact — it names what the first sentence's action amounts to. By writing a poem about a sculpture, Falconer is performing ekphrasis and thereby joining a tradition that reaches back to Homer. The transition has to point back at that action and label its consequence, which is what "In doing so" does.

whyWrong.A: "In addition" would introduce a second, separate activity, but participating in the ekphrastic tradition is not something Falconer does besides writing about the sculpture — it is that act, described differently.
whyWrong.C: "That said" signals a qualification or reversal, and nothing in the second sentence pulls against the first.
whyWrong.D: "Conversely" marks an opposite case, but the two sentences describe the same act from two angles.

tips: When the second sentence restates the first act at a higher level of generality, look for a transition that refers back to that act rather than adding to it.

whyCorrect: The sentence before the blank gives one reason Hilo suits the role of state soil — it is abundant across the state. The sentence after the blank gives a second reason — it supports agriculture and grows crops like ginger and taro. Two reasons pointing the same way call for an additive transition, and "Additionally" is the only one on offer.

whyWrong.A: "Alternatively" presents a competing option instead of the previous one, but the agricultural role does not replace the abundance argument.
whyWrong.B: "By contrast" signals opposition, and both reasons support the same conclusion about Hilo.
whyWrong.C: "At that time" points to a moment already established in the text, and no time frame has been given.

tips: Two supporting reasons in a row almost always take an additive transition, not a contrastive one.

whyCorrect: Both sentences make the same point about different people: Albert Popa used an "unconventional surface," concrete, and his son David has chosen an "unusual canvas," ice floes. The parallel wording is the giveaway. A transition marking similarity is what the slot needs, and "Likewise" supplies it.

whyWrong.A: "However" sets up a contrast, but father and son are being shown to share a habit, not to differ.
whyWrong.B: "Indeed" intensifies or confirms the previous statement, yet the second sentence introduces a different artist and a different project rather than reinforcing the claim about Albert.
whyWrong.C: "Second" would number items in a list the writer is enumerating, and no such list has been announced.

commonMistakes: Reading the shift to a new person as a shift in direction; a new subject doing the same kind of thing calls for a similarity transition.

whyCorrect: The stated goal is to emphasize the number of medals, so the sentence has to put the totals front and center. The notes give two figures: eighteen medals in all, sixteen of them gold. Choice B is the only option that states both numbers, and it frames them as a career total.

whyWrong.A: "Multiple gold medal wins" replaces the exact figures with a vague quantity, so the emphasis on number is lost; it also garbles the date range.
whyWrong.C: This gives the sixteen golds but buries them in a clause about swimming's history at the Paralympics, and it drops the eighteen-medal total.
whyWrong.D: This mentions no medals at all and instead defines what the Paralympic Games are.

tips: When the goal names a quantity, prefer the choice that keeps the actual numbers rather than a word like "multiple" or "many."

whyCorrect: The goal is similarity, so hunt through the notes for something the two works share. Their dates differ, their sizes differ, and their material lists differ — but acrylic appears in both: "acrylic and oil stick" for Untitled (Two Heads on Gold) and "acrylic, oil, graphite, crayon, and paper collage" for Jazz. Choice C is the only option that isolates that shared medium and states it of both works.

whyWrong.A: This gives the two completion dates, which are different, so it points at a difference rather than a similarity.
whyWrong.B: This says one work is larger, an explicit comparison of difference.
whyWrong.D: This lists the two material sets side by side, and the contrastive "while" pushes the reader toward how the lists differ rather than what they share.

tips: When two lists overlap only partially, the shared item is usually the answer to a similarity question — read the lists element by element.

whyCorrect: The goal is to give a specific example of a slow TV program, so the sentence must name an actual program. Only choice B does — Nordlandsbanen: Minutt for Minutt — and it also shows why the program qualifies, describing the uninterrupted 10-hour real-time broadcast of the Trondheim-to-Bodø train ride.

whyWrong.A: This names a scholar and her book, not a slow TV program.
whyWrong.C: This defines the genre and mentions train rides generically, but it names no particular show.
whyWrong.D: This quotes Wheatley's characterization of the genre as a whole and again names no specific program.

tips: An "example" goal is satisfied only by a named instance; a definition of the category, however accurate, does not count.

whyCorrect: The colon means everything after it defines the blank, and what follows is a picture of constant change: a "constantly evolving" network of channels and land strips that "change in size and shape" as new sediment arrives. A word meaning always in motion is required, and "dynamic" is exactly that.

whyWrong.A: "Sustainable" concerns whether something can be maintained over the long run, a question the sentence never raises.
whyWrong.B: "Unrivaled" means without equal, but the sentence opens with "As with other river deltas," placing the Krishna alongside others rather than above them.
whyWrong.C: "Immutable" means unchanging, the direct opposite of the constant evolution described after the colon.

commonMistakes: Picking "immutable" because it sounds technical; check its meaning against the evidence after the colon, which describes continual change.

whyCorrect: Read what the action accomplishes: Gogol tips his head back "in order to see" a kite so high it is a speck against the sky. To look up, you tilt your head backward, so "tip" here describes a physical movement of the head. "Lean" is the choice that names that motion.

whyWrong.B: "Inform" is the sense of "tip" in "tip someone off," but you cannot inform a head, and no information is being passed.
whyWrong.C: "Pay" is the sense in tipping a server; it takes a person as its object, not a body part.
whyWrong.D: "Produce" has no connection to any sense of "tip" and does not fit an action performed to see something overhead.

tips: For vocabulary-in-context items, substitute each candidate into the sentence literally; only one will leave the described action physically possible.

whyCorrect: The clause after "thereby" tells you the result: investors can stop worrying about bureaucratic detail and turn their attention to business opportunities instead. For that shift to happen, the worries have to be reduced. "Assuage" means to ease or lessen a concern, which is the only choice that produces the stated effect.

whyWrong.A: "Designate" means to assign a name or role, which cannot be done to worries.
whyWrong.B: "Amplify" means to increase, so investors' anxieties would grow — the opposite of freeing them to focus elsewhere.
whyWrong.D: "Convey" means to communicate or transport; knowing about oversight does not transmit investors' worries anywhere.

tips: The word "thereby" links cause to effect — read the effect first, then choose the verb that could produce it.

whyCorrect: The next sentence paraphrases the blank: "Once wearing clothing turned into a widespread, familiar practice." So the blank must mean widespread. "Ubiquitous" means present everywhere, and it is what allows the shift the argument depends on — only when everyone wears clothing can differences in clothing carry social meaning.

whyWrong.A: "Divisive" means causing disagreement, but the argument is that clothing became common first, and social meaning followed from that commonness.
whyWrong.B: "Provisional" means temporary, which contradicts a practice becoming established and familiar.
whyWrong.D: "Feasible" means possible; clothing was already being made and worn at these sites, so the change described is in how widely it spread, not in whether it could be done.

tips: When the following sentence restates the same idea, treat it as a definition of the blank and match a choice to its wording.

whyCorrect: Both examples describe artists mixing categories that are supposedly separate: Choctaw hymns folded into folk-pop, Indigenous flute and powwow vocals set against electronic music. Artists who blend across a boundary are refusing to treat that boundary as binding. "Reject" is the verb for declining to accept the distinctions.

whyWrong.A: "Disguise" would mean concealing the distinctions, but these artists foreground both traditions rather than hiding either one.
whyWrong.C: "Observe" in this sense means to comply with, which would have the artists honoring the separation their work crosses.
whyWrong.D: "Replace" would require them to substitute something for the distinctions, but no new category is offered in place of the old ones.

commonMistakes: Reading "observe" as "notice"; in this construction it means to abide by, which reverses the point the examples make.

whyCorrect: Track the passage in three moves. It opens broadly — three million shipwrecks worldwide and researchers' general interest in their ecological effects. It then narrows to Hamdan's specific study, including the pine and oak samples placed at set distances from two Gulf of Mexico wrecks. It closes with one result: peak microbial diversity around 125 meters out. General interest, specific study, single finding — that is choice B.

whyWrong.A: Nothing says the study received significant scholarly attention, and the text reports the researchers' own findings rather than anyone's reaction to them.
whyWrong.C: The San Pedro's historical significance is never described; it is named only as one of the three million wrecks.
whyWrong.D: The pine and oak are sampling materials the researchers placed on the seafloor, not the wood the ship was built from, and no famous wreck's construction is discussed.

commonMistakes: Assuming the pine and oak describe the shipwreck itself; reread and you will see the researchers positioned those pieces at measured distances from the wrecks.

whyCorrect: The text opens by defining convergent evolution, then reports Sucena's work on convergence through a shared genetic mechanism and Wittkopp's on convergence through different mechanisms, and finally notes that Green and Extavour took up both types in one 2012 study. Definition, two studies, a third study — that is the structure choice D names.

whyWrong.A: No widespread assumption is stated, and nothing in the text argues that any assumption is unfounded.
whyWrong.B: The order is wrong — the two earlier studies come first — and the text critiques no one; it says only that the relative prevalence of the two routes remains poorly understood.
whyWrong.C: The text does not trace a field's development over time and offers no speculation about future research; the third study is already published.

tips: For structure items, count the moves in order and match them one by one; a choice that gets the sequence backwards is wrong even if it names the right pieces.

whyCorrect: The passage opens by saying women "made important early contributions" to US cryptology, then supports that with Blum's Army work, her NSA career, and her role in moving the agency to computers, and closes by connecting her to later women in the field such as Baginski. The main idea has to be the contribution of women to cryptology, which is what choice B states.

whyWrong.A: The definition of cryptology is background given in the first sentence; the passage is about the people, not the field's scope.
whyWrong.C: Nothing says Blum and Baginski worked together — Baginski is presented as someone whose entry Blum's generation made possible, and she works in the present.
whyWrong.D: The passage makes no recommendation about school curricula or about how to recruit women.

commonMistakes: Choosing the sentence that defines the topic; a definition given as setup is rarely the main idea.

whyCorrect: Watch what shifts and what stays fixed across the three sentences. The companion changes each time — the captain, then the second mate, then "one other man," then nobody at all — but Harris is unfailingly among the few who were not ill. The narrator is quietly pointing out that Harris revises his story while the flattering part never varies.

whyWrong.A: The passage says nothing about how Harris spent his time; it lists who else supposedly stayed well.
whyWrong.B: Harris is not struggling to remember and no friends are questioning him — he is volunteering anecdotes, and the shifting details read as embellishment rather than confusion.
whyWrong.D: Harris describes a past crossing, and nothing indicates he fears rough water on the current trip.

tips: When a passage repeats a claim with one element changing each time, the point is usually about the teller's reliability.

whyCorrect: The hypothesis is comparative: in low visibility, intermediate-headed fish should detect large-vortex obstructions more often than wide-headed fish do. Support therefore has to test both head types under those conditions and show the predicted gap. Choice B does that — the wide-headed devil catfish collides with obstructions more often than the intermediate-headed rainbow trout, which is what worse detection would look like.

whyWrong.A: This measures only the wide-headed species, so there is no intermediate-headed group to compare it against; "more than half" means nothing without a baseline.
whyWrong.C: Equal collision rates would show no difference between the two head shapes, which undercuts the hypothesis rather than supporting it.
whyWrong.D: Variation among individual trout says nothing about how intermediate heads compare with wide heads.

tips: A comparative hypothesis needs comparative evidence — reject any finding that reports a single group's performance in isolation.

whyCorrect: The claim has two parts: Winnemucca speaks directly to the reader, and she does so in order to explain a custom. Choice A satisfies both — "Now, my dear reader" is the direct address, and the rest of the sentence explains why her people call good people father or mother. No other option pairs the address with an explanation.

whyWrong.B: This describes the naming custom but never addresses the reader, so half the claim is missing.
whyWrong.C: This is narrative background about her grandfather and a birth; it neither addresses the reader nor explains a custom.
whyWrong.D: This addresses "dear readers" but explains nothing — it declines to describe the scene and leaves it to the reader's imagination.

tips: When a claim joins two features with "to," verify both separately; most distractors supply exactly one.

whyCorrect: The rival explanation the passage names is communication with members of the same species, so support has to tie the sound to the attacker rather than to an audience of peers. Choice A does that by timing: no species produced sound before the attack, and nearly all fell silent within ten seconds after it ended. A sound that appears only while a threat is present and stops the moment it passes is behaving like a signal aimed at the threat.

whyWrong.B: Species-specific sounds are exactly what you would expect if the calls were for members of the same species, so this points toward the explanation the researchers are arguing against.
whyWrong.C: This says only the clicks fall in a range predatory birds can hear and that the vocalizations do not, so it undercuts the claim for one of the two sound types the study recorded.
whyWrong.D: Variation in which sounds individuals make says nothing about whom the sounds are aimed at.

commonMistakes: Assuming any detail about predators supports a predator-directed claim; a finding that covers only part of the recorded sounds and excludes the rest is mixed evidence.

whyCorrect: The word "However" marks the surprise. Being ingested inside a host normally shields complex life cycle parasites from the outside world, so you would expect them to weather warming better than directly transmitted parasites, which are exposed during transmission. The data went the other way: three-host CLP abundance fell while directly transmitted abundance held steady. The conclusion has to be that whatever protection the CLP strategy offers was outweighed by other temperature-driven pressures, which is choice B.

whyWrong.A: This says more host species means better protection from warming, but the parasite requiring three hosts is the one whose numbers declined.
whyWrong.C: This claims ingestion-transmitted CLPs depended less on warming-affected hosts, which cannot explain why those very parasites were the ones that declined.
whyWrong.D: The passage states the opposite about shielding — CLPs are the ones typically protected during transmission, while directly transmitted parasites are exposed.

tips: When a passage sets up an expected advantage and then reports the opposite outcome, the completion usually says the advantage was outweighed rather than denying it existed.
